Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.summary: Google Workspace now offers native support for Markdown (.md) files, allowing developers and AI agents to seamlessly collaborate on documentation directly in Google Docs without manual file conversions. This integration preserves native file fidelity for use with Git repositories and developer tools while unlocking standard Docs features like line-level commenting, rendered Drive previews, and tracked version history.

Under the theme "Build, Secure, Scale," participants gain hands-on experience with Google’s developer stack—including Gemini, Google AI Studio, Google Antigravity, and Web MCP—through live workshops and codelabs. The conference focuses on enabling developers to prototype rapidly, ensure secure and private deployments, and leverage production-ready infrastructure.

items.title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
items.summary: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.

items.title: Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats
items.summary: A2UI now supports swappable inference formats, introducing A2UI Express which uses up to 3x fewer tokens and cuts latency by compiling compact Python-style syntax into standard A2UI JSON via Agent SDKs. Developers can also use controlled generation with TypeSafe's Jev system-decision models to render known-shape screens in under 300 ms while smaller models stream text. These updates require no changes to frontend renderers or component catalogs, offering flexible performance levers for generative UI development across Python, TypeScript, and Dart.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon
items.summary: Google Research has completed the 32-bit open-source Coral NPU RISC-V architecture with the introduction of its Matrix Execution Unit, which delivers up to 1 TOPS while targeting 10 mW average power for edge inference. Alongside this architecture, the release of the v1.0 open-source IREE/MLIR compiler allows developers to take models from JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow straight to Coral NPU hardware without writing custom assembly. Developers can now prototype and deploy these multimodal edge applications using new hardware options like the Synaptics Astra SR200 MCU series and globally available Coralboard devkits.12

items.title: Bringing Visual Graph Debugging to Custom Edge Compilers with Model Explorer
items.summary: Google AI Edge Model Explorer now supports custom compiler intermediate representations and open-source adapters like TOSA, VGF, and PTE for on-device machine learning. Developers can leverage hierarchical graph visualization, split-pane views, and per-node trace overlays to catch export regressions and verify hardware delegation. These tools enable engineering teams to transparently debug execution graphs and pinpoint cycle-level latency bottlenecks locally.

items.title: Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec
items.summary: API Gateway now supports real-time streaming—including Server-Sent Events, WebSockets, gRPC, and chunked transfer encoding—in Public Preview without requiring changes to your existing API specifications. This update allows developers to route long-lived, bi-directional streams and AI workloads directly through the gateway while maintaining consistent authentication, rate limiting, and observability. Additionally, gateways now feature deterministic default hostnames, simplifying environment provisioning and infrastructure-as-code management.

items.title: Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services
items.summary: LiteRT in Google Play services now offers GPU inference powered by ML Drift, delivering about 1.4x faster performance alongside the new CompiledModel API. Switching from bundled binaries reduces app size by approximately 8 MB while enabling seamless, automatic runtime updates across billions of devices. Developers can easily adopt these updates by updating their dependencies and utilizing the new Android Studio LiteRT skill for automated migration.

items.title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
items.summary: A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across web, mobile, and desktop applications. Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. The release introduces bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding to help teams seamlessly integrate generative UI into their product stacks.

items.title: Architecting Governed, Self-Evolving AI Agents on Google Cloud
items.summary: Learn how Project Chrysalis combines Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Agent Development Kit (ADK), BigQuery, and a four-gate defense-in-depth security stack (Model Armor, Cloud KMS, Binary Authorization, and OPA) to build governed, self-evolving AI agents that remediate live production outages in 1.8 seconds.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation
items.summary: This post walks through the Agents CLI evaluation loop for systematically improving agent performance through continuous testing and grading. It demonstrates how to catch prompt regressions, evaluate model backend swaps using side-by-side trace comparisons, and automate evaluation passes. Developers will also learn how to integrate nightly scheduled runs with threshold-based alerting to track quality over time.

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: Voxels aren't LEGO: teaching a brick packer to build like a person
items.summary: When you ask an AI for "SpongeBob's house in LEGO", the hard part isn't the shape. The hard part is that a shape made of cubes isn't a LEGO model. Real builders don't stack 1×1 bricks into a block. They cross the layers so they lock, use one big plate for a base, leave the inside hollow, and use as few kinds of parts as possible, so you can actually collect them. This post covers the packer I wrote for Mister Blocks, and the rules it learned, mostly from me looking at a build and saying "nobody would build it like that". Bluey's Queenslander house: 128 pieces, 15 steps. One of the LEGO buildings the packer made. A build is described as a stack of layers. items.title: Moving my portfolio from a Vite SPA to Next.js
items.summary: A while ago I ran curl against my own portfolio and got back half a kilobyte of HTML. The only visible text in it was the page title: 17 characters. My experience, my projects, the links to my articles, all of it was rendered in the browser by JavaScript. For visitors, that was fine. For a LinkedIn link preview, an ATS crawler or any bot that doesn't run JavaScript, my portfolio was an empty page called "Mehdi's Portfolio". Every route shared that one title, with no description and no Open Graph tags. The site was a React 19 SPA built with Vite, routed with react-router and deployed on Vercel, with a rewrite sending every path to index.html. I moved it to the Next.js App Router so every page ships as real HTML. This post is about the parts that turned out less simple than I expected. I gave myself a single constraint: same content, same design, pixel for pixel. If a migration "mostly looks the same", you stop noticing what broke. items.title: I Built My Own RSS Reader in an Afternoon, With AI Doing the Typing
items.summary: For years my RSS setup was a compromise. I never wanted to pay for a desktop reader, so I stayed on The Old Reader: a perfectly fine service, but it felt like visiting a website, because that's what it was. What I actually wanted was simple: a native Mac app, feeds stored locally, no account, no subscription, and fast enough to triage a hundred articles from the keyboard. So I stopped wishing and built it. LumenAI is a local-first RSS reader for macOS with AI summaries, taken from an empty folder to a notarizable DMG in about an hour of wall-clock time, with me as product owner and build verifier while the AI wrote the code. My pitch to the AI was one paragraph: a local RSS reader for Mac, a premium feel, and treat it like a real engineering project, with clear phases, and ask me questions before making decisions. That last sentence mattered most. Instead of a wall of code, it interviewed me: stack, what v1 includes, what it excludes, how refresh works, what "premium" means concretely. In 2016 I shipped a small arcade game for iPhone and iPad called Coocader. It had some ads, never really took off, and I moved on to other things. The code sat untouched for almost ten years. This autumn I decided to bring it back. Not as a remake, but as the same game, modernized properly. A few weeks later, version 1.1 is live on the App Store. This is the story of how that went, what broke, and what working with AI as a pair programmer was actually like. Coocader is inspired by Space Invaders, with one twist: blocks with silly little faces move down toward your ship, and you can only destroy a block with a shot of the matching color. So you're constantly switching colors while aiming. Some blocks have shields, some shoot back, some drop gifts that help you… or ruin your run. If a block reaches the bottom, it's game over. React and Next.js can send the bytes directly to S3-compatible storage; the application server should decide who may create, read, replace, or delete a receipt. A browser upload should carry a file and a temporary capability. items.title: Node.js Cron Setup: 2 Periodic Database Cleanup Patterns for Webhooks
items.summary: Short answer: use a Node.js cron setup that claims due database cleanup rows with a lease; use a durable queue only when retry backlog and replay controls justify the extra state machine. A cleanup job in a logistics backend should be boring: claim old rows, make one bounded attempt, record the result, and leave the next run enough information to recover. For outbound shipment webhooks, that means a retry must never turn one delivery into two customer-visible state changes. The least complex setup is a single Node.js worker process triggered by a scheduler, with the database as the source of truth for claims and idempotency. A cron expression alone cannot provide delivery semantics. It only provides a chance to run code. That is the boundary. Scheduling is not delivery. items.summary: A vocabulary flashcards app is a small app that shows you a word, lets you guess its meaning, and flips to reveal the answer — and building one is one of the best JavaScript projects for a beginner. It teaches you the skills every real app needs: storing data, rendering one card at a time, handling clicks, and shuffling a deck so you never memorise the order. If you know basic JavaScript and want to learn new English words while you build, this project does both at once. How does it work? You keep your words in an array of objects — each one has a word, its meaning, and an example sentence. Buttons let you move to the next card, go back, or shuffle the deck, and a small counter shows your progress — card 3 of 20, for example. You save your words in localStorage, so your deck is still there when you close the tab and come back. That is the whole app: data, rendering, flipping, and storage. Find every place a version is pinned: global.json, Dockerfiles, CI pipeline SDK versions, build scripts. Check what your machine and pipeline actually resolve: dotnet --list-sdks dotnet --info Check your dependencies for outdated or abandoned packages: dotnet list package --outdated Run your test suite on the current version and save the result. items.title: How to compute US banking days in JavaScript
items.summary: I shipped a settlement-date bug that only appeared on a Friday in July. The date was 3 July 2026, the day before Independence Day, which falls on a Saturday that year. My function marked that Friday as a bank holiday because that's what most "US federal holiday" libraries do. Federal offices are closed. Federal Reserve Banks are not. If you calculate ACH or Fedwire settlement dates, you need the Reserve Bank calendar, not the Office of Personnel Management calendar. They diverge whenever a holiday lands on a Saturday. For payments, a US banking day is a weekday when Federal Reserve Banks are open to operate FedACH and Fedwire. Retail branch hours are a separate question, and the Board of Governors in Washington can close on a Friday when the Reserve Banks themselves stay open. I care about the Banks, because that's when settlement happens. The official list is published by Federal Reserve Financial Services. I used that 2026–2027 schedule rather than generating dates from rules of thumb. C# is a strongly typed, object-oriented language: you define classes, create objects from them, and use methods to make them do things. The syntax is clean and readable, with curly braces and semicolons like Java and JavaScript. With .NET, you get a huge standard library, so common tasks — reading files, talking to a database, or building a web API — take very little code. items.title: Node.js Object PUT vs Multipart Upload — Pick Multipart for Large App Backups
items.summary: Short answer: use multipart upload for large Node.js backup archives, and keep the upload ledger in your job database so a worker can resume, complete, or deliberately abort the transfer. The deciding constraint is throughput under interruption. A developer-tools platform may turn thousands of receipt images and records into one tar.gz, then retain that exact file for an audit. Holding the archive in memory or restarting one giant PUT after a broken connection makes the retry unit needlessly large. Multipart changes the retry unit from “the whole audit archive” to “one numbered part.” This is an operational choice, not a promise that multipart wins for every object. Small receipts can stay on a single PUT. Large backup bundles should not. Picture the original worker as a three-box diagram in words: archive file -> one request -> object storage. If the request stops near the end, the next attempt returns to byte zero. The application also has no durable record that distinguishes “never started” from “partly transferred.” It is easy to draw. items.title: SaaS Error Event Query API in Node.js (with Rollback-Safe Imports)
items.summary: Use a queryable error event API plus a separate schedule monitor when a Node.js SaaS marketplace needs alerting for imports that stop producing results. The decision rule is strict: advance an import watermark only after the result is durable, and make alert delivery retryable without letting notification state rewrite that watermark. A thrown error is evidence of one failure; missing expected output is evidence that the workflow itself may have stopped. TL;DR: emit structured start and terminal events from the Node.js worker, store them behind a small query API, and run an independent cron monitor that compares each schedule's deadline with its last successful result. Send Slack or email through an idempotent outbox. This design makes silence observable, preserves an audit trail, and lets a deployment roll back without erasing or duplicating the operational truth. A marketplace import has at least three clocks: the scheduled start, the worker's actual start, and the durable completion. items.title: Stop trusting file extensions: validating uploads by content (with ffmpeg)
items.summary: A user of my free tool uploaded a recording named voice.m4a and got "This doesn't look like a real .m4a file." The file was fine. items.title: Cutting a Next.js page from 854 KB to 459 KB of HTML by weighing the RSC payload
items.summary: My /projects page in Next.js 16 shipped 854 KB of HTML for a list of 49 projects. Almost all of that weight was the same few strings repeated, and in the App Router every repeat ships twice: once as HTML and once more inside the inline React Server Components payload (the self.__next_f.push scripts at the bottom of the page). Three changes took it to 459 KB: an SVG sprite for the icon on every row, JSON-LD that links to detail pages instead of copying them, and named Tailwind utilities for the row classes. A fourth stopped the page from prefetching 36 routes it didn't need. Open view-source on any App Router page and scroll to the bottom. After the HTML you will find self.__next_f.push([1,"..."]) scripts. That is the RSC payload, the serialized component tree React uses to hydrate the page and to navigate without a full reload. Every element a server component renders appears in it as data, props included. So a server component that renders an inline 49 times puts that path in the document 98 times. Tom's Hardware reports: As for Logitech, the company believes that it's time for people to move away from the belief that playing games is a waste of time, hence its new initiative. It makes sense for a company that makes gaming accessories to say that, of course, but CEO Hanneke Faber argues that the company sees "how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other." The hope will be that, by allowing employees to play games, a productivity boost will follow. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Apple Is Killing Its Support Community Forum Next Week
items.summary: Apple is shutting down its Apple Support Community forum on November 20, ending a user-to-user support platform whose history stretches back to the 1998 launch as the Apple Tech Exchange. The forum is already read-only, and Apple has not said whether the nearly three decades of community posts will be preserved or disappear when the site closes. Here's the full banner notice that's currently displayed on the website: "The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site. We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products." Apple told MacRumors that it decided to sunset the forum after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.summary: A teleprompter that scrolls as you speak sounds simple: recognize speech, find the words in the script, move the text. I built that for iOS and the recognizing part was the easy part. The hard parts were making the scroll feel calm and not trusting the recognizer too much. Here is what I learned. Disclosure: this is my app, Teleprompter Offline & Private. I use Apple's speech recognition and require on-device mode. If the language has no on-device model, the app says so instead of silently falling back to a server. That choice makes the app work in Airplane Mode and means your voice never leaves the phone. The cost: some languages need the offline speech pack, downloaded once in iOS settings. The recognizer returns a stream of partial transcripts. I align them against the script with a fuzzy matcher that searches a lookahead window of 40 to 70 words past the current position. Fuzzy, because people skip words, say "gonna" for "going to", and the recognizer mishears. The scroll jerked. I spent days tuning easing curves. items.title: Your UI should tell you what's going on
items.summary: I opened a budget app last month to check one number, how much I had left to spend, and I could not find it. The balance was on one screen, the spending was on another, and the budget was a third screen with a tiny progress bar I had to squint at. I knew the data was in there somewhere, the app had it, it just was not showing me. I closed it and did the math in my head instead, which is the exact moment a UI has failed at its job. I keep coming back to a line from Ben Halpern's post, ask more of your UI. The idea is simple: a UI should act like an instrument panel, showing you what is going on, live, instead of hiding the state behind taps and menus. A car dashboard does not make you open a menu to see your speed. It is just there, all the time, because the whole point of the dashboard is to tell you where you stand. I built a little budget tracker to try the idea out, nothing fancy, just a panel that shows the four things I actually check. Balance, spent this month against the budget, the next bill coming up, and whether the data is synced. Every number updates the moment something changes, so the panel is always current. We expose REST endpoints, define gRPC contracts, implement business services, establish integration patterns and build applications that consume these capabilities. The API-first approach has served us well. It has enabled distributed systems, microservices, platform engineering and ecosystem integrations. But something fundamental is changing. AI is no longer just another feature that we integrate into an application. items.title: Free Currency Converter API for iOS and Android: Swift and Kotlin
items.summary: A free currency converter API is easy to call from a mobile app. Doing it well takes three more things: the app must work offline with the last known rates, it must tell the user how old those rates are, and the API key must not be inside the app binary. This guide covers all three, with working code for iOS in Swift and Android in Kotlin. The examples use the AllRatesToday rates endpoint, which returns mid-market rates for 160+ currencies, refreshed every 60 seconds. An iOS or Android app is a file the user downloads. Anything compiled into it, including an API key in Info.plist, BuildConfig or an obfuscated string, can be extracted with free tools in minutes. Once extracted, the key works from anywhere until you rotate it. So the app never talks to the rates API directly: The app calls https://rates.example.com/rates?source=USD&target=EUR,GBP,JPY on your own backend. The backend adds Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY, calls AllRatesToday, caches the answer and returns the same JSON array. items.title: A compiler that refuses a contract that says too little
items.summary: A compiler that refuses a contract that says too little This article was written with the help of an AI assistant (Claude), like the language it describes, which was built with Claude Code. I checked every figure against the repository and I take responsibility for the content. It follows Green proofs, empty promises. In my previous article I asked a small model to write verified Dafny. The proofs were green. But 5 of the 8 contracts barely constrained the result: a length, a format, a shape. One of those methods was wrong, and the proof did not notice. A verifier proves what it is asked to prove. If the same agent writes the code and its contract, it can ask for exactly as much as it manages to prove. Checking the proof is not enough; the question is whether the contract says enough. I built a small language, Quod, to try one rule: the compiler asks whether two different results could both satisfy the contract. Your feeds, categories, settings, read articles, and starred articles all go through a single, small Apple API: NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore, the iCloud key-value store. The whole thing fits in less than 1 MB. This post explains how the store works, why I picked it, and the tricks that keep NewsNinja inside its limits as the app has grown. The first version of NewsNinja was a very simple RSS reader. The only thing that needed to sync was the list of feeds you subscribed to, and a feed list is just a list of URLs. For that, a real database felt like overkill. Core Data or SwiftData would have meant a schema, a model container, migrations, and a CloudKit container to set up and maintain, all to store an array of strings. items.title: From idea to the App Store in a weekend: a medication reminder built in November 2026
items.summary: On Thursday evening at 20:40 I opened an empty folder with a short note: remind me to take my pills, let me confirm I took them, keep a history, count what is left at home. On Friday at about 16:00 the app was submitted to App Store review, for iPhone, iPad and Mac, in four languages. On Monday morning Apple approved it. The app is Vzato ("taken" in Czech), and it is in the App Store now. It is free, open source under MPL-2.0, has no server and no accounts, and syncs through the user's own iCloud. The code is on GitHub. I built it with Claude Code. This post is about what that looked like in practice: why I built it, how the day went, what I did and what the AI did, and what it means to write and ship an app like this now. It wasn't magic, and it wasn't a toy either. There are plenty of them. I tried several before this, and none of them worked for me. Some I did not like. Some I simply did not understand how to use. And most of them missed small things that matter a lot when you actually take pills every day: When can I eat? Some medication has to be taken on an empty stomach, 30 minutes before food. So the reminder I need is not only "take your pill", it is also "you can eat now"

items.title: Return or throw? Result pattern vs exceptions in ASP.NET Core
items.summary: The order does not exist. Now what? Every .NET API answers this question many times a day, and there are two camps. One throws a NotFoundException and lets something upstream turn it into a 404. The other returns the error as a value. Both work. Both have real costs. This post lists the pros and cons of each, shows numbers, and ends with the rule I use. TL;DR Return the errors a caller can expect: not found, conflict, validation failed. They are 4xx. Throw what should never happen: a bug, a dead database. It is a 500. You need both, and both should produce the same error shape. public async Task GetAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct) { var order = await repo.FindAsync(id, ct) ?? throw new NotFoundException($"Order {id} does not exist."); return order.ToDto(); } Somewhere else, an IExceptionHandler or a middleware catches NotFoundException and writes the 404. It is built in. Every .NET developer knows it and every library already uses it. The happy path stays clean. There are no checks after each call. It cannot be ignored by accident. items.summary: Point a general camera translator at a page of raw manga and you get one of two results. A single paragraph of English in an order that makes no sense, or one tiny box per column of text, each translated on its own, so nothing reads like a sentence. I build Yomi, an iOS app for reading manga that only exists in Japanese, and most of the work turned out not to be translation at all. It was geometry: deciding which pieces of text belong to the same speech bubble, in what order to read them, and where to put the English afterwards. This post is about that part. Three things a sign or a menu never does to you: Vertical text. Japanese bubbles are usually written in columns, top to bottom, and the columns read right to left. OCR engines tend to return each column as its own line. Many separate blocks. A page has eight to fifteen bubbles. A translator that treats the page as one block of text merges dialogue from different characters. Small text at page scale. A whole page photographed by a phone leaves each glyph a few pixels wide. items.title: Why a plain FFT tuner locks onto the wrong note, and what I used instead (McLeod Pitch Method on iOS)
items.summary: I'm a solo developer at a small studio, and I recently shipped a guitar tuner and metronome called Maestro. The tuner was the part I got wrong first, so this post is about that. The obvious way to build a tuner: take a window of microphone samples, run an FFT, pick the tallest peak, convert to a note. It works on a sine wave. On a real guitar it doesn't, because the loudest bin is often the 2nd or 3rd harmonic, not the fundamental. A low E (about 82 Hz) will happily read as the E an octave up, or as a B, depending on the pluck. MPM computes a normalized square-difference autocorrelation of the window. Instead of looking for the biggest peak in frequency space, it looks for repeating structure in time, and normalizes by signal energy at each lag so quiet tails don't lose to loud attacks. Then it picks the first strong peak, which is the fundamental, and refines it with parabolic interpolation for sub-sample precision (this is what gets you to a fraction of a cent). items.title: Open Core in a Public Repo: Gate Paid Features With License Keys, Not Secrecy
items.summary: Your repository is public. Anyone can read the paid modules, fork them, and build them. So what actually separates the Community edition from the paid one? In open core and Fair Source projects the answer is not code secrecy. It is the license key: a signed entitlement that tells one self-hosted installation which paid features it is allowed to use. This post walks through how to design that boundary so it stays fair to operators and practical for you. Classic open core keeps the core under an open source license and puts commercial modules in a separate directory (often ee/) with their own terms. Fair Source goes a step further: the commercial code is readable, but the license limits certain uses of current versions and converts to a permissive license later. Keygen moved to FCL, and Directus announced an FCL-derived license for v12 together with registration keys for paid users. items.title: Building a Thread-Safe Concurrent List in C# from Scratch
items.summary: While .NET provides powerful thread-safe collections in the System.Collections.Concurrent namespace—such as ConcurrentDictionary and ConcurrentQueue —it notably lacks a built-in ConcurrentList . If you have ever needed to read and write to a list from multiple background threads simultaneously, you quickly realize that standard collections like List fall apart under concurrent pressure. In this article, we will build a custom, production-grade ConcurrentList from scratch in C# using ReaderWriterLockSlim, explore why dynamic lists are chosen over fixed arrays, test it with a multithreaded stress test, and analyze the performance costs involved. When multiple threads read and write to a standard List concurrently, several issues arise: Data Corruption: Interleaved writes corrupt internal array capacity tracking and element pointers. Race Conditions: Two threads inserting at the same index simultaneously will overwrite one another, resulting in lost data. Exceptions: Modifying a collection while another thread is iterating over it throws an InvalidOperationException. items.title: M John Harrison Becomes First Sci-Fi Author To Win Booker Prize
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Eighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award's history. Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison's was "the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world." She called it "a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page". Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the 50,000-pound award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening. The End of Everything, Harrison's first Booker nomination, is set a few decades from now, years after a disaster nobody can properly account for. Set on the Kent coast, the novel sees Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie attempting to survive alongside the looming threat of the mysterious iGhetti: vast, shape-changing beings whose origins and intentions are never explained. items.title: Swarm (/swarm) (10 minute read)
items.summary: The /swarm command in Google Antigravity runs a team of named agents that split tasks, work on the pieces at the same time, and coordinate on one shared message board. It can be used for tasks that divide cleanly across separate files, packages, or questions, or when a second agent is needed to review and test the changes before a human sees it. The /swarm command is available on Google AI Pro and Google AI Ultra plans in the Google Antigravity App and Antigravity CLI. Every worker is its own agent, so swarms use quotas much faster than single conversations.

items.title: Google Fi Brings Back Network Switching With 'Secondary' Partner
items.summary: Google Fi is bringing back network switching through an unnamed "secondary" 5G carrier. "Most users will be on the 'Primary network,' but Google Fi will automatically switch users to the 'Secondary network' if it meaningfully improves performance with so-called 'smart thresholds' for doing so," reports 9to5Google. "At launch, there is no manual switching." When Project Fi first launched the service included support with both Sprint and T-Mobile. That went away when T-Mobile acquired Sprint in 2020. 9to5Google reports: Google is not naming the second network today, but did share that Ultra Wideband is supported. Officially, you are switching between "two of America's fastest 5G networks." Fi Wireless does note that users have top priority, so data is never deprioritized on the Primary network. Meanwhile, there's "highest QCI priority" on the backup network that means subscribers are among the last to be slowed down when there's congestion. This is also available internationally when local partner networks are available with the Flexible and Unlimited Premium plans. Network switching will first be supported on Pixel 9 and newer devices that have a Google Fi eSIM (and no other SIM act

items.title: Fireworks AI Confirms Wider Breach Affecting Notion AI Chats

Notion, the popular productivity and note-taking app, disclosed that it was impacted in the breach but "fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces" were involved. "Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable," it said. "'Unattributable' means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results." The Hacker News reports: In a notice published on October 10, 2026, [Fireworks AI] said it detected unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials that allowed an unauthorized third-party to access environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. items.title: New York Launches Nation's First State AI Testing Program
items.summary: New York is launching a state-backed AI safety research center at Binghamton University that will independently study and test AI systems, develop safety and security techniques, and train researchers in responsible AI. "While the federal government fails to act, New York is leading the way on AI safety and holding big tech accountable," New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said. "The stakes are too high to simply take AI companies at their word." Politico reports: The center -- which is funded by a $30 million gift from Bloomberg co-founder Tom Secunda and a $25 million research investment from SUNY and New York state -- is set to launch before New York's major AI safety law, the RAISE Act, comes into effect on Jan. 1. That will require submissions of detailed safety frameworks from AI companies operating in New York State, which Hochul's office hopes will be scrutinized by researchers at the new center. "AI is opening up questions that scientists could not tackle before," said Secunda, who also serves as the board chair of Empire AI, a $500 million public-private partnership. items.title: Starlink Mini 2 Adds a Swappable Battery, Wi-Fi 6
items.summary: SpaceX has unveiled the Starlink Mini 2, equipping the company's smallest satellite internet terminal with a removable 71Wh battery and Wi-Fi 6. Preorders are opening to select U.S. customers for $999, which also includes a year of Roam Unlimited service. Shipments are expected to begin in mid-December. InterestingEngineering reports: The removable battery represents the biggest functional upgrade over the original Starlink Mini. Previously, users needed an external power source to operate the satellite terminal. That meant carrying additional equipment for camping trips, remote work, or extended journeys. Mini 2 addresses that limitation with a detachable 71 Wh battery pack. It weighs approximately 1.08 pounds (490 grams) and delivers up to 4.5 hours of connectivity. Owners can replace it with another charged battery when necessary. The battery also features LED indicators and its own USB-C charging port. SpaceX supports 60-watt USB-C Power Delivery charging for the pack. The retail kit includes a compatible 60-watt wall adapter and a three-meter USB-C cable. items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
items.summary: A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

items.title: ‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity
items.summary: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed ‘I am a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book 12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know everything we do is a fiction until it’s a fact: the dream of flying, the dream of space travel, the dream of speaking to someone instantly, across time and space, the dream of not dying – or of returning.” She had already been thinking about our possible futures for at least 15 years – her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, for instance, imagined a post-climate catastrophe world populated by robots and humans who never age, while 12 Bytes was preceded by Frankisstein: A Love Story, which alternates a recreation of the summer Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein with a trans doctor’s travels among present-day cryogenecists and AI-enabled robots.
